newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu supports independent Bank of Israel.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu supports independent Bank of Israel.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday affirmed his support for an independent central bank one day after a marginal interest rate cut provoked widespread outcry among business and political leaders.

"Modern economies have all gone to a state of independence and I'm not going to try and change this. The independence of the central bank is important," Netanyahu told a conference of exporters organised by the National Export Institute.
"In the long term we would make a terrible mistake if we would undermine this very basic principle."
On Monday the Bank of Israel announced a 0.3 percentage point cut, bringing its key lending rate to an annualised 15.2 percent.
Business leaders, especially exporters, argued that a far steeper cut was needed to restore profitability at a time when Israel's economic growth is slowing sharply.
Amir Makov, chairman of the export institute, called for immediate monetary measures such as a further rate cut to correct the shekel's exchange rate, which is hurting exporters.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said that until fiscal policy is tightened, monetary policy must continue to restrain.
"I don't think the Finance Ministry or the Bank of Israel can decide what to do based on reasons of popularity," he told exporters.
"As long as fiscal policy is expansionary there is no choice but for monetary policy to restrain."
He said it would not be easy for the government to implement the necessary budget cuts but if it succeeds, "fiscal conditions will be far more comfortable for monetary policy".
Frenkel repeated his stance that the government's proposal to cut 4.9 billion shekels from next year's budget would not be enough. "I believe we are going to have to cut more," he said.
Netanyahu also said a further cut was likely due to a shortfall in revenues this year.
Frenkel said budget cuts were a step in realising the goal of reducing inflation to levels prevalent in industrialised countries, noting that in today's world economies are interdependent.

Frenkel said a real depreciation of the shekel would help profitability. But he argued that trying to change the exchange rate by lowering interest rates would provoke only a nominal, not a real, depreciation of the shekel.

"By printing money you don't create a real devaluation. You create a nominal devaluation that is quickly eroded and you are left with the problem of higher inflation and...you don't solve (the problem of) profitability."
Netanyahu reiterated that the government next month will present a multi-year plan for privatisation as well as a programme for structural reforms to increase competition.
